parts.note: surface reading: a business whose ledgers or a band whose discs earn a profit
setter's reading: a coin-operated machine full of gramophone discs takes cash for every song it plays

explanation.surface: Someone's accounts or chart hits turn a healthy profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Records' tempts you towards accounts or a recording artist; think of the café machine that plays a single for a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A coin-operated music player stocked with singles earns cash each time a customer chooses a song.

clue.text: One drink that refreshes, but another will be a different matter

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a single serving of the British national beverage
second meaning: the idiom 'another ___' means something quite different

explanation.surface: One reviving drink is welcome, but a second may be something else altogether.
explanation.walkthrough: In British idiom 'that's another cup of tea' means that is a quite separate matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A single serving of the hot brewed beverage refreshes; the idiom with 'another' denotes something entirely distinct.

clue.text: Transport for student with a university final

parts.note: L for learner, the plate a student driver displays
with means together with, i.e. and
taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university, placed last

explanation.surface: A student needs a lift to the university's final exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Final' only says the university's letter comes at the end. A landau is a four-wheeled carriage with a folding hood.
explanation.definitionFit: A landau is a horse-drawn carriage, an old-fashioned means of conveying passengers.

clue.text: Factory shutdowns designed to cure loss

indicators.note: something designed is planned and laid out afresh, so the letters are arranged into a new pattern

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Shutting factories is a plan meant to stop the company losing money.
explanation.definitionFit: When a plant is shut down permanently, that event is one of these, a ceasing of operations.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a very brief instant of time
second meaning: significance, as in 'of great ___'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Second in importance' reads as ranking runner-up; split it into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a brief instant ('just a second') and weight or significance, as in matters of great consequence.

clue.text: Homeless city female pleased to be settled in compartment

indicators.note: settled in describes one thing lodged within another, so the word for pleased sits inside the word for compartment

parts.note: a bay is a compartment, as in a loading or bomb bay
glad means pleased

explanation.surface: A homeless woman in town is happy to have a corner of her own to settle into.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a homeless woman in a town who carries her possessions around in shopping bags.

parts.note: surface reading: in fine voice, singing at a high pitch
setter's reading: piping as a set of pipes, so shaped like a tube

explanation.surface: A singer or bird is in shrill, high-pitched voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piping' suggests a shrill voice, and 'in form' suggests fitness; read it as having the shape of pipes.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything shaped like a tube or cylinder, as plumbing pipes are.

clue.text: Athlete who's out of place on the track

definitions.text: Athlete who's out of place on the track

parts.words: Athlete who's out of place on the track
parts.note: surface reading: a sportsman who doesn't belong in a running race
setter's reading: finished outside the first three placings, so unplaced

explanation.surface: A sportsman looks like he has no business being on the running track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of place' means unplaced, finishing outside the medal positions, not misplaced.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a competitor or racehorse that failed to finish among the winners, hence any loser.

parts.note: surface reading: heads of the armed forces
setter's reading: table service in a restaurant, whose chiefs run the dining room staff

explanation.surface: The heads of the army, navy and air force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service chiefs' points to generals and admirals; the question mark sends you to restaurant service instead.
explanation.definitionFit: These senior restaurant staff supervise the others who serve diners at table.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sixtieth of a minute
the runner-up position in a race

explanation.walkthrough: 'Time and place' sounds like the stock phrase about suitable occasions; it is two meanings joined by 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a short unit of duration and also the runner-up ranking behind the winner.

clue.text: Daisy enters city from the west

definitions.note: heading eastwards, i.e. travelling from the west

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so the flower goes within the city's name

parts.note: Ely is the cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A girl named Daisy arrives in town after a journey from the west.
explanation.walkthrough: Daisy looks like a woman's name. EASTERLY of motion means towards the east, so travelling from the west; of wind it means the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Describing movement, the adjective means heading towards the east, which is coming out of the west.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: soldiers who fight on ___, as in the ___ Guards
second meaning: the bottom of something, as of a hill or page

explanation.walkthrough: 'Infantry base' reads as an army camp; it is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word denotes foot soldiers collectively, and also the lowest part or bottom of anything.

parts.note: surface reading: a substitute on a sports team's bench
setter's reading: an actor in the theatre who learns a role in case the lead cannot go on

explanation.surface: A substitute waits on the bench for a chance to play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' suggests sport, but the player here is an actor.
explanation.definitionFit: This actor learns a principal's part so as to stand in when the regular performer is unavailable.

parts.note: surface reading: the name of a Royal Navy vessel
setter's reading: London is a capital, so a vessel named after it is a ship of the capital

explanation.surface: A Royal Navy warship bearing the name of Britain's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: A capital ship is a navy's largest class of warship, such as a battleship; London is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: The term names a navy's biggest, most heavily armed vessels, and a ship called London honours a capital.

clue.text: Says again that the treatise needs amending

indicators.note: amending means altering or correcting, so the letters must be changed into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone repeats the point that a scholarly essay requires revision.
explanation.definitionFit: To repeat a statement or perform an action once more is the meaning of the verb, from Latin for 'again'.

parts.note: an iron is a type of golf club
a side is a team

explanation.surface: A strict Puritan signs up with a golf club's team.
explanation.walkthrough: Ironsides was the nickname of Cromwell and his Puritan cavalry in the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: Cromwell's Parliamentarian troopers were nicknamed this, so the singular names one such stern religious soldier.

parts.note: surface reading: wipe away every bit of evidence
setter's reading: traces are the straps attaching a horse to a cart, so take them all off

explanation.surface: A criminal cleans up so no evidence is left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Traces are the side straps of a harness by which a horse pulls a carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: To free a horse from the vehicle it pulls you release its harness straps; the verb means to unfasten.

parts.note: surface reading: an inappropriate topic for a nursery class
setter's reading: Sheridan's play is titled The School for ___

explanation.surface: A lurid topic unfit for a group of toddlers at nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: The School for Scandal is Sheridan's 1777 comedy; 'play school' is also a British phrase for a nursery.
explanation.definitionFit: Shocking gossip or a disgraceful affair is this, and it gives its name to Sheridan's famous comedy of manners.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: natural and free of pretension
second meaning: unaltered, not influenced by something

explanation.walkthrough: 'Just the same' looks like 'nevertheless'; here it means unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means both unpretentious in manner and not influenced or changed by some event.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: fells someone with a blow, as a boxer does
second meaning: levels of a building

explanation.surface: A demolition crew brings down a building several levels at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to send someone sprawling, and the plural noun names the levels of a multi-storey building.

clue.text: Find company in one churchman or another

indicators.note: in places the word for company inside the word for one kind of clergyman

parts.note: a dean is the senior clergyman of a cathedral
Co is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: One clergyman or another goes looking for companionship.
explanation.walkthrough: The first churchman is the shell; the result is a second, different churchman.
explanation.definitionFit: A deacon is an ordained minister ranking below a priest, so a different kind of clergyman from a dean.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: formerly, as in 'the ___ king'
second meaning: on a single occasion

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen is the only difference: one sense is former, the other is a single occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means formerly or at some point in the past, and also on exactly a single occasion.

parts.note: surface reading: a brute famous for stubbornness
setter's reading: literally having the head of a bull

explanation.surface: A notoriously obstinate brute refuses to give way.
explanation.walkthrough: Bull-headed usually means stubborn; take it literally for the beast of Greek myth in the Cretan labyrinth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this creature, half man and half bull, lived in Crete's labyrinth until Theseus killed it.

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor
something posted has been sent

explanation.surface: A seaman is officially listed as missing in action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posted as missing' reads as a military notice; split it into its pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone missing is not present where expected, which is what the adjective means.

clue.text: A trip with passengers, we hear, makes profits

definitions.note: loosely, builds up as gains do

indicators.note: we hear says the words are to be taken as spoken rather than as spelt

parts.note: a cruise is a sea trip carrying passengers

explanation.surface: A passenger cruise turns out to be a money-spinner.
explanation.definitionFit: When interest or gains accumulate over time, money builds up and increases, the sense of the verb.

clue.text: Some degrees short of actual conflict?

definitions.text: Some degrees short of actual conflict?

parts.words: Some degrees short of actual conflict?
parts.note: surface reading: a hostility that stops a few steps before open fighting
setter's reading: a low temperature, chilly rather than hot

explanation.surface: Relations between rivals stop just shy of open fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: Degrees look like stages of escalation; read them as temperature, so the hostility is chilly, like the post-1945 US–Soviet standoff.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the long postwar rivalry between the Soviet bloc and the West that never became open fighting.
